utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. De Grave, if I understood you correctly, from the X-rays taken in 2001, it is possible to conclude that in the case of Mitar Vasiljevic, the fractures occurred as indicated in the case history issued by the hospital that you have just reviewed. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: Yes. They are perfectly compatible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also found traces of traction on the X-rays. My question is whether your examination of Mitar Vasiljevic's leg also showed such signs. Is it possible to establish any such signs of traction?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: The small mark on the outside cannot be seen, but on the inside one can see under the skin, under focused light, a small, round mark with a diameter of, I think, if I'm not mistaken, of 3 or 4 millimetres. So it can be seen. That is true, yes. But let me also add that one of the X-rays, we put a pen on the mark, and a photograph was taken of the point of the pen, which showed the trace on the bone of traction. So there is a connection between the outside and the inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Groome asked you about the standard procedure for filling in case history forms such as the one you have in front of you. Are you familiar with the standards that used to be applied, especially in those days, that is almost ten years ago, in Yugoslavia, or is what you are saying based on the standard procedure in your country, that is, in Belgium?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: It is international, and these are not minor details. This is an essential element, and it is a custom that was introduced at the beginning of the nineteenth century by the TransAmerican Railway Company, which was the first to issue files on victims and labour accidents and occupational accidents. And so this procedure was established with the establishment of the railways, and it is applied by all administrations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. De Grave, you were talking about a military document and the military, the army. I would just like to draw your attention to the fact that this document which is before you, and it is Exhibit P62, or 136 of the English version, is a document issued by a civilian hospital, not a military hospital. It is a document that is issued for civilians and not for military men.

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: First of all, I haven't seen the official document, the original document, but only the translation. That is my first point. The second point, if you have an accident, as a civilian, you do the same thing. I have told you that is a universal procedure applied everywhere. So when there is a responsibility in question, one is going to discuss the circumstances under which an accident occurred, and that is why this is so important. So it doesn't apply only to military documents but also to civilian ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. In this document where the date and hour of the injury should be filled in, nothing has, in fact, been filled in, and we really don't know why that wasn't done, whether the practice should have been applied to all cases or not, but I thought you were talking about military hospitals and military forms. My question is whether a form of this kind, though this is a translation and it is difficult for you to say whether it is an internationally acceptable form or is it a form specially adapted to local circumstances in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: I think that anyone can compile documents. I'm not familiar with the customs, but generally speaking, the entries are entered from left to right, from top to bottom, but what is essential are the data, which are the same in -- perhaps entered in a different order, but the data are usually the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. De Grave, have you had occasion to review a copy of the discharge document issued by the same hospital of the 6th of May 1993? And the diagnosis is refractura cruris sinistra. So a little less than a year after this first injury dated the 14th of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: No. I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If this is a repeated fracture of the same leg, is it possible for the fracture to occur in the same place or, rather, if it is in a different location, would there be traces on the X-ray -- your X-rays, of 2001?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: One may refracture on an average within a period of two years. If there is a refracture, repeated fracture, it will always occur in the same area, and generally it is possible to note the refracture in the structure, but there is no guarantee, if it occurs within a two-year period, of the vertical structure. Let me explain with the help of an X-ray that we have here on the screen. We can -- if we see the compact, it is regular, and there is an enlargement here, and on the other hand, we see again a small enlargement. And here there is a trace, a mark, which corresponds to a temporary pseudo-arthrosis. One must not forget that he was exposed to traction and there is -- that is why a fracture under traction requires much longer time to treat than if it is put in a plaster cast. So we see traces here. The X-ray of the fracture tells us a story. And I see on this fracture -- I do not see elements that lead me to suspect a second fracture. After a period of two years, it is almost impossible for the fracture to occur in the same location. That would mean that my fracture was -- my treatment was defective and then the fracture would occur above or below the original fracture, but we don't see that either. Therefore, regarding your question, I haven't seen the dossier, and this is in my first report, all the documents that I had, and I'm not aware of this document, but to answer your question, I don't see any evidence to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, Doctor, it is possible that, in the case of a repeated fracture that occurred within a period of less than a year since the first fracture, that such a refracture could have existed and that your X-rays from the year 2001 do not exclude that possibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you should make it a reasonable possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps having interfered with it I'm sorry, Mr. Domazet, but it is important. I think what Mr. Domazet is after, Doctor, is this: Is it a reasonable possibility that a further fracture occurred within 12 months and that it just doesn't show on this X-ray?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there was a further fracture within that time period, one should not forget that it is a fracture in an area which is already of inferior quality. In our technical jargon, we say that it is an affected area. So if there is a second fracture, one can see additional traces, and also the treatment is more difficult. If there is a further fracture within this period of two years, one would have to undertake surgery of one kind or another, and one would also see external traces on the bone, exetosis, or rather, deformations. And I have to say that the fracture that I see on this X-ray was a big fracture and was finely treated without any reduction in the physiology or the quality. It's a magnificent treatment that was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'll leave it to you, Mr. Domazet to follow that up. There is something, I think, to follow up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. De Grave, yes, you explained regarding fractures that would occur after a period of two years. But this was not the case here. And I am just interested in the possibility of a further fracture within a period of less than one year since the original fracture. So is it possible that such a further fracture occurred without this being specifically visible on the X-rays you took in 2001?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: No, if you're talking about a refracture. We are talking in that case of difficulties of recovery, because that is the same thing. And if there is a refracture, you see an additional swelling. Just a moment, please. I'll take another reproduction. One would see traces, a broader, a larger kortex. You would see irregularities. This fracture was treated in one go. There was no disruption. This is very clear. It was fully healed. The only thing that you see as a result of traction is this mark, but there is no element in the X-ray that lead me to suspect that there was a refracturing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. De Grave, in your written report, in the part on the discussion and answer to questions, there is a question as to: Can you see whether the leg was fractured one time or more than once? Your answer is: "No, after more than two years, we can't see whether the leg was fractured once or several times or more than once. It is possible that the two bones of the lower leg were broken separately in different orders." What I have just read out, does it differ from your previous answer? Because it seems to me that it does.

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: I'm just looking for that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that same page, may I read a little further on, where it says: "When a second fracturing incident of the lower leg happens, in the not too distant future, and certainly within one year, that fracture shall overcome on the same location as the first fracture."

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: One should not forget that you are asking me questions which are very difficult. One sees a bone that has been fractured and healed. One sees only one fracture. And you're asking me hypothetical questions and that is the difficulty. We know very well that if there is a second fracture, it may occur, but the question was: Can one see where whether the leg was fractured one time or more than once? I said no, but what I see on the X-rays, we have a fracture that is quite regular, that has been healed regularly, and that is why one does not ask oneself whether there was a man on the moon or not, whether you can see a second fracture. There are no elements to lead me to say that the fracture was irregular, in which case one would ask, what is the source or the reason of that irregularity? We don't see any irregularity. And that is why there is a conflict in my perception of these questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are mentioning as one of the arguments the fact that the bone healed well. Could that good healing have occurred after the repeated fracture, the second fracture?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: Oh, no. You are operated on and you have a scar and then you're reoperated in the same scar so as to avoid having two scars but you can see that. It is not possible to redo a scar or a fracture in the same location, in the same place. That is the dream of aesthetic surgeons. They are trying to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to me, then, what I have just read out in relation to what I have asked? Because otherwise, I really don't see the -- don't understand the meaning of this written answer.

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: Which text?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If necessary, I can read it again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Page 19 of your report, doctor, under heading: Discussion and answer to the questions. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Page 9, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, page 9, yes, page 9. And it's the third question: "Can one see whether the leg was fractured one time or more than once?" And Mr. Domazet read out to you part of the paragraph which follows that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you, and I apologise for saying this, if one reads the question and also my answer [in English] "was fractured one time or more than once." [Interpretation] It's a theoretical question and my answer was a theoretical one, but if we look at the reality, then the question does not arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But doctor, you were answering the question regarding this particular case. And later on, on that same page, you can find verbatim, and I quote, "When a second fracturing incident of the lower leg happened, in the not too distant future, and certainly within one year, that fracture shall overcome on the same localization as the first fracture." What does this mean, then, this answer? What does your answer mean?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: What is the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is, whether this second incident that you mention, is it a refracture or a repeated fracture of the leg? Because there is no other incident that we could have been referring to.

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: You're talking about a second incident. I did not study a second incident. I didn't see a dossier about a second incident. I only saw one X-ray and one dossier, one file. You're asking me questions about something that is quite unclear to me, unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, what Mr. Domazet has read to you is under the next question on the same page, "can one estimate in what year," et cetera, and the third paragraph of that is the passage which he read to you: "When a second fracturing incident of the lower leg happens, in the not too distant future." What Mr. Domazet is asking you what do you mean by that other than that there could be a second fracture within the one year at the same point. Is that right, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When one sees an X-ray ten years later, one sees that there was a fracture. One has a picture, and this picture, which I explained a moment ago, has a certain structure. And if we are dealing with a refracturing in the same localisation, it cannot be seen. If it is a fracture that has a certain continuity, without any new elements, the picture will be of a single fracture, so it is very difficult to distinguish. I have pointed to a mark on the X-ray, whether that mark is due to difficulties of immobilising the first fracture or was it a fracture that was reactivated by a second incident, that is something that one cannot see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think if we go back to Mr. Domazet's original question, then, is it reasonably possible that there was a second fracture or a refracture at the same point within 12 months? Looking at that X-ray. That's the 2001 X-ray.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm repeating what his original question was, and I think we are led back to it. Is it reasonably possible, looking at that X-ray, the 2001 X-ray, that there may have been a second accident and there was a refracture at the same point? Is there anything on the X-ray which prevents that from being a reasonable possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, the question is rather rare, because we are talking about the fracture of Mitar Vasiljevic and not the fracture of a hypothetical person. So the X-ray we have is an X-ray of the fracture of a person in good condition regarding the healing of the fracture. When you have another fracture before the completion of the ossification, it cannot be seen. If there is a fracture after the ossification, then one will see it. One should not forget, there are few people who know that a bone when it breaks, it consists of two elements, the structure, a protein structure and cells deposited in that structure. So the protein structure, like all protein structures, heals within ten days. When you cut your finger, that cut is closed soundly after about ten days. The recovery of that lesion, in the case of a cut of your finger, will actually last weeks. And for the bone, there are deposits of calcium, phosphates, et cetera, that need to be recovered. So the process is not completed. It is the protein structure that dominates, which is very soft and flexible, and that is why if a fracture occurs again within a certain period of time, one cannot see it. As soon as the deposit of calcium has developed, and one has another fracture, you see fragments that can be seen. So that is the answer to the question. Also, the difficulties that I described in my report, because the time limit is two years, the bones in the case of Mr. Vasiljevic, was a good quality bone, with a capacity of restoration that was of high quality as well. So a period of two years applies generally, but I think in this case, it should be much less. Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic is not a hypothetical person. He's a man of flesh and bones, a real man, in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can I just ask one question arising out of that? I feel like a politician when I ask that question. Doctor, ossification, that is the new bone developing where there has been a fracture, is it? And that is the process which takes 12 months or two years?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: Not two years, a few months. In normal conditions, the time limit is three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Because you said in your previous answer, if there is a fracture after the ossification, then one should see it. So it's a few months, the ossification process? I'm asking that because I thought you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had originally said two years.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, I don't know how to put it. Ossification, the restoration of a bone, is one element, but ossification of a fractured leg is achieved by a swelling, a callous, as it is called, and this callous is additional calcium deposited around the fracture, and this calcium may be remodeled, among other things, by muscular activity, and this activity is achieved on an average, it is not restrictive, after two years. After two years, one can say that the calcium has been deposited and the fracture has been remodeled and it is completed. So that would be the date, time limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly, then, doctor? It is within this period of two years that that is possible, that is to say the time limit within which we speak that a refracturing was possible?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, we can say that. We can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question, Dr. De Grave: In view of the concrete situation, this fracture with traction, fracture plus traction, which is the case in hand, on the basis of your report, in a hospital of that type, traction would have to last six weeks, and after that period of six weeks, after a plaster cast has been worn, the fracture can be reduced and then you use a word, you use a term, which is probably not English, and all this is accompanied by a six-week recovery period. Does that mean that you consider that six weeks were necessary, six weeks of traction, plus six weeks of wearing a plaster cast and at least six weeks of rehabilitation after that? Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: I listened to you, but the question eludes me. Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of your written report dated the 26th of August, you state the following: "In regional hospitals, and when there is a shortage of medical materials, a traction throughout six weeks, followed by six weeks in a plaster cast, can replace the reduction of the fracture by means of a," something I can't read, "Kuntchner nail," you say, whatever language that is. Then it says: "This all will be followed by six weeks revalidation at least." Do I understand you properly that in a fracture of this kind, traction lasts six weeks, plaster cast is a further six weeks, so six plus six weeks for a plaster cast, and finally at least another six weeks for rehabilitation? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: Well, let me say at the outset that this is a question, an empty question, in a vacuum, asked in a vacuum. Had I not had the other documents, I wouldn't have known. I couldn't answer that. But as I have had all these documents at my disposal - and I mention all the documents that I have - if I don't mention the documents, it means I haven't seen them, so I mention the exact number. What you're asking me is a theoretical question. Now, if we decide, if we look at the traction, the traction needed for a good result, then we would say you need six weeks. But looking at the file that you sent me, I see that it was actually done for three weeks. That is the half of six weeks. But this would be a theoretical answer. And I'm interrupting you here to say that in medicine, the question of dates and measurements is an aetherial one. We don't deal with dates and measurements. We look at the medical entity, the object, and if we start discussing dates and measurements, centimetres and so on, in a void, in a vacuum, we can't get the right answer. But if you wish to obtain a result with the application of a Kuntchner nail, then that takes a long time and that is the important thing to note. That Mr. Mitar had six -- three weeks of this, I am not surprised. I know of some cases where it took even less time. So there we have the differences. But that wasn't the question that you asked me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more point, Dr. De Grave, although this might be common knowledge to laymen as well, but I think it would be a good idea for you to tell us. When we deal with traction in cases of this kind, does that mean immobilisation, that the patient has to lie in bed immobile with weights on their legs, with the impossibility of any kind of movement even within a hospital room or a room?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: That is our goal, the goal we wish to attain, immobilisation, to immobilise somebody, but not only to immobilise them but to keep the different elements in the proper position. For example, very few people know this, but if you have a fractured leg, and we decide to place a Kuntchner nail on it, before we place the Kuntchner wire or nail we introduce a Kirschner nail in your heel to position the leg properly, and once we have placed the Kuntchner nail, we withdraw the needle. So this is not only the case for immobilisation purposes but to keep the leg in the proper position. I read in the file that the gentleman liked to drink alcohol, and I am fully conscious of the difficulty this presents with people who like drinking, who are very thirsty. To keep them in a bed, immobilised, I think this would be martyrdom, both for the patient and his physician. So we try to keep him in bed for as short a time as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart -- unless the therapy does not include alcohol as well. Is that possible for the therapy to include alcohol?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: I don't know. There are poseotox medicaments, that we call, and they contain a certain amount of alcohol in them. So that would be an alcohol intake of sorts. And I see in the papers that I have before me, and I'm leafing through them very quickly, that he had an abstention crisis three or four weeks afterwards, which means that he's not going to wait three or four weeks to drink alcohol. He must have had some alcohol intake in the first or second week, because he used up all his reserves. So he would have entered into a delirium -- delirious state, and doctors would have been able to see that very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Dr. De Grave. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I don't know whether you are going to call evidence on this issue about the interpretation of the X-rays, but if you are, you have an obligation to put the nature of the case you propose to make in your evidence to Dr. De Grave to enable him to deal with it. It shall save having to call him in reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour. If I decide to do that, I will inform you on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you're not able to do it at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Groome? Re-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. De Grave, Mr. Domazet has asked you or put to you some information regarding a possible injury of the accused in 1993. And the question that I have for you is, just looking at the X-rays that were taken in August of 2001, are they as -- are they also consistent with a single fracture to the -- Mr. Vasiljevic's leg occurring from an injury in 1993?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: [In English] Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question: Is it possible for you, simply looking at the X-ray taken in 2001, to tell us whether that fracture occurred in 1992 or 1993? Are you able to tell, just looking at the X-ray, the date at which the fracture occurred?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: I think that the file, document 62, is quite clear. It describes a victim that was admitted to the emergency ward with a tibio-fibulary fracture. So I think that your answer is contained in that document, the answer to your question. It is a tibio-fibial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, you are being asked from the X-ray alone, the X-ray in 2001. Forget about this case history, what happened to somebody in 1992. From the X-ray, are you able to say whether the fracture you see there occurred in 1992 or 1993? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One final question. Assuming Mr. Domazet's proposition that Mr. Vasiljevic may have broken his leg two different times, assuming that proposition, would it change your position whether the leg shown in X-ray from 1992 is not from the same person as the 2001 X-ray?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: The X-ray of 1992 is another -- of another person. We can't compare something that doesn't belong to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even if what Mr. Domazet is saying were to be true, that the -- Mr. Vasiljevic's leg was broken two times, is it still your opinion that the leg depicted in X-ray 1992 is of a different person than the leg of Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: The 1992 X-ray shows a fraction of a tibia not of a fibula and the 2001 fracture shows a fracture of two legs. Two legs. No. I'm sorry, I meant two bones. 1992 there was one bone, not two. In 2001, there were two bones, two fractured bones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is still your opinion at this time that the legs depicted in or the leg bone depicted in the X-ray from 1992 is that of a different person than that of Mr. Vasiljevic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, I wonder if you could explain some of the terms you've used because I'm afraid like all doctors, you forget that we do not speak the same language. I mean medical and legal. A refracture, a refracture does that mean a fracture in exactly the same spot and along the same fault line, if you could use that expression?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: The same place or almost the same place. There is a slight nuance there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, if there had been one in almost the same place, would it have shown up on this X-ray?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: We could see it. Now I'm going to answer by giving you an example. You take an object, for example, and it is a plastic object, hard plastic, and you break it, and you stick it back together again with glue, stick it back together again with glue, and for some other reason it breaks again, you're going to have it break in the same place. You can have the same fracture. But after you stick it with glue, you will see these glue fragments, supplementary glue fragments on the spot where the fracture has taken place. I don't know whether I'm being clear. The same thing happens with a bone. If it is fractured and restored, and let me take it a step further, if it has been restored more than 72 hours later, we -- you will see those same small fragments when it is restructured. Does that answer your question? I could of course go into the reasons why that take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we want to know the reasons at this stage any way. What I'm concerned about is the meaning of this word refracture, which was a very careful word used by Mr. Domazet in his question. Is -- if a refracture does not break along the same general direction as the previous one, but it is somewhere close to it, would that be shown on the -- would you expect to see that on this 2001 X-ray?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: On a standard X-ray that we usually use, you could hardly see it, barely see it, but if we suspect that it is there, then we can adapt and calibrate the machinery used to have it reappear. That is why, when giving an expert opinion, experts do not content themselves with radiograms, X-rays in general. Usually they ask for new X-rays and say very precisely what they are looking for in fact. So if we suspect that there might be certain difficulties or errors, then we start to research into them and we ask for more data. And if we look at the heel that we took up and we took, made several X-rays of the heel. Those X-rays were taken under different conditions. We changed the voltage, for example, and we changed the exposition time, exposure time. And then we looked at the legs and the X-rays taken in March, for example, in the detention unit, which were of poor quality, but they were taken in different conditions. We took our own X-rays. And then we looked to see if there were any irregularities that -- and if you don't -- if they don't come out on one X-ray, they might come out on another. One X-ray will show the structure of, how shall I -- what is the term, let me see, the bony structure, the direction of the crystals. You can see that on certain X-rays and not on others. Which means that if we suspect something is there, if our attention is drawn to something, then we pay special attention to the details. And that is the difference between X-rays taken by the treating physician, he wants to know what the fracture is, and what is the best way to treat and restore that fracture. What we are dealing with, it is not our job to restore the fracture. We are researching into the structure of the fracture. And I did not see any irregularities that would be suspect. So that is -- brings me back to the question. Refracturisation, refracturing, if there is something that draws our attention and we are suspicious then we would go into it further, as I described a moment ago, when giving the example of the object that was broken and stuck together again. There is always some debris or fragments from the glue at the place of the fracture, of the rupture, and we can see that debris, if you will, or fragments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean if you had been warned that this was an issue, you would have used a more sophisticated form of X-ray? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: Among other things, among other things, but it's not necessary here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, if you had been told that Mr. Vasiljevic was asserting that on the 6th of May 1993, he fractured his leg again about three centimetres below the old fracture, would you have done some different form of X-ray investigation?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Even without that different type of X-ray examination, would you have expected to see on the X-rays you took in 2001 another fracture three centimetres below the old one?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: I would be somewhat surprised to be able to see -- to encounter that. It would require special techniques. We would have to go to Professor Zingoff in Brussels or Dr. Blaka [phoen] in Blaskat [phoen]. I don't think it can be done here. That is the first point. My second point is that I would be a little bit surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Surprised about what? You would be surprised that you had not seen it or that you would be surprised to see it?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: To be quite frank, we didn't look at the X-rays and I can say that for seven days they were on my apparatuses, on display, and I looked at them several times at different times, to see anything that could possibly be on them, and I consulted Dr. Bollen and two other physicians. We studied the X-rays together. And we described in our reports what we saw on those X-rays, and we didn't see any elements which would lead us to suspect refracture. Other elements that were there, we did describe. We mentioned -- make mention of them but there were no elements that would lead us to think of that, to suspect anything like that. There was nothing on the basis of which we would say, "Well, look, there is something here," which would alert us to any such situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm still trying to ascertain what you mean that you would have been surprised. Are you saying that if there had been another fracture three centimetres below the old one, within a year of the old one, you would have been surprised that you had not seen it on the X-ray, or that it could have happened and you had seen it?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: We would have seen slight irregularities. We would have seen them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now the next thing you raise, you said he only received three weeks' traction according to the case history. I'm just wondering where you got that from. You see, on the 15th of June, it says that the Kuntchner wire was pulled through the heel and a device with a 7 and a half kilo weight is attached to it. I would assume that that was the beginning of the traction.

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, where do you say the three-week period ends?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: It was put under traction on the 15th of June, and then it was taken off on the 7th of July -- discharged, sorry, discharged on the 7th of July, and I don't believe that one would discharge somebody under traction. He wouldn't be able to walk with traction, walk home with the traction. And this is the 7th of July document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see, yes. The date of discharge is the 28th of July. 28th of July, 15th of June? That's more than three weeks, isn't it, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's referring to an entry on the second page dated the 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: [In English] Wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The only entry I have there is a discharge order on his way out out, and it goes on to say on the 17th he had a cast fixed, this is all still in hospital, and according to the front page of it, the discharge was the 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe the doctor was referring to that entry but we can ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Okay. Now, doctor, for those who have not had any experience of hearing orthopaedic issues, what exactly is a Kuntchner nail or wire?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: Kirschner, yes. We make the same mixture between Kuntchner and Kirschner. It's in a U-shaped nail, a U-shaped nail. A real Kirschner is a very special device, but it is very often reproduced because the real one, the real Mccoy, is an expensive one. So the real one is in the form of a U, and you bend it slightly when you place it inside, into the body. And then under the effects of bodily pressure, it opens up. So it is a way of fixation. It pulls the bone together on the leg, and it is enough to use a Kirschner to fix the upper and lower portion, and it will remain in the same place. It is a fairly long nail, 35 to 40 millimetres in length. And I have photographed, for example, a kneecap, a knee. And you can see this on the photograph, and I have a reason for which I took these photographs. For example, here, you can see a promontory, and if you bend your knee, if you bend your knee, you will see this, you will see that there is a protrusion of some kind. Now, this protrusion can be taken off with a device, you can make a hole and introduce the Kirschner. But once you've placed the Kirschner there, or once you try to place -- to introduce the Kirschner, you can see that because there is a swelling. That is to say the swelling disappears, the protrusion disappears. Whereas we have the Kirschner needles as well, and they are four millimetres in diameter, of different lengths. You can have shorter ones, longer ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I was more concerned with the one we had here and I'm sorry if I mispronounced it. Now, finally, doctor, in your answer to Mr. Domazet, when he was asking you about a refracture at one stage, you said something along the lines that you would have expected there to be operative treatment after a second fracture or a refracture, and that you saw no signs of that. Now, what did you mean there?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: In that case, refracturing, for that, one would have to nail -- screw in a piece of metal from the outside, using nails, screws. You would screw it in and fix it in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is after a refracture, that's what you would expect to happen?

utterances.speaker: YVAN DE GRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, after refracture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see. Now, Mr. Domazet, do you want to ask any questions out of my questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not really, Your Honour, except in connection with this case history. It shows that during treatment, Mitar Vasiljevic was transferred to the psychiatric ward. So it is true there was no indication whether traction continued in that ward, and that is probably why Dr. De Grave mentioned three weeks, because that would roughly correspond up to the date when he was transferred to the psychiatry ward, where he remained until the 28th of July. But I hope that we will be able to clear that up through Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you want to ask any questions, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. De Grave, for your attendance and for your evidence. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until 2.35. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, after the difficulties we had getting Dr. De Grave to answer the questions, it's obvious we are running a bit behind time. It's important we finish today so that we can get Mr. Domazet off to prepare for his case to begin the week after next. How much do you think is left in this witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would anticipate 15 minutes of examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Will you be very long with him in cross-examination, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, there is only Mr. Roy left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour and then introduction of some 92 bis statements and some other documents on consent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, that won't take long. If I might make a small plea or warning whatever you like to the people in the booths and the Court reporters, it may be necessary just for 15 minutes or so if we can sit on this afternoon so that we will not lose a whole week's hearing. But we'll see how we go. Thank you. Yes. Well, sir, you're still bound by the oath you took before. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we start with this witness there is just one Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. matter coming from Dr. De Grave's testimony. Prosecution tender and it was accepted into evidence the original X-rays Exhibits 21 and 151. As we all is saw, it was more appropriate to use the photographic version of those, so I am suggesting that perhaps a consent with Mr. Domazet that we substitute the actual photographs of those X-rays. So for Exhibit 151, that we substitute the photograph that Dr. De Grave had, and that's page 4 of his first report, and the photograph of Exhibit 21 was entered into evidence as 21.1. I would suggest that the Prosecution at this time withdraw the actual X-ray, Exhibit number 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. I was a little surprised to hear the doctor say that he had had access, he had had custody of Exhibit 151 all of this time. As I understand it, the order was that they be made available to the Defence if they wanted an expert to view them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And they were, Your Honour. They were available any time Mr. Domazet requested them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. But why did Dr. De Grave have them? He lives outside Antwerp somewhere and you can't go and pick them up easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was just in his custody until one of us could go down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Obviously they weren't needed in this time, but it's just as well. You proceed, Mr. Groome. Examined by Mr. Groome: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 84, I apologise for the delay in resuming your testimony. Yesterday, you concluded your testimony at the point in time when you're inside the house by the creek. I want to draw your attention to a particular time when you were in that house. Did there come a time when you were aware of a fire inside of that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what first brought your attention and what first made you aware of such a fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The flame coming from the door and spreading towards the house, the interior of the house. The only thing I could do was to make those three steps to reach the window. Once I reached the window, my mother was at the window. She was breaking the window. I pushed her into the creek, a shrapnel from the bomb hit me in the forehead. I have a little scar there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at the time the fire broke out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the middle of the house. I was sitting on the kitchen table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you characterise for us the intensity of that fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very high intensity and it was spreading fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there much smoke from that fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time -- or you testified about receiving an injury from shrapnel. Was there an explosion inside of the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was already at the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you were at the window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explosion occurred when the bomb was thrown into the house and the shrapnel hit me on the forehead. I have a scar on my forehead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see who threw that bomb inside the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after the bomb exploded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I jumped out with my mother into the creek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far was the creek from the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About three metres approximately. Very close by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go from the creek?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went along the creek. There was a big tree, and we hid behind that big tree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that anyone else jumped out of that same window behind you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew of person under number VG38, that she was at the window next to me. But when exactly she jumped into the creek, I have forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you mentioned going to a big tree. What did you do at that tree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We hid behind it. We were in hiding there, because immediately they came round to the side where the window was and started shooting, so if anyone were to jump out, they would kill them. And they shone their flashlights on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see the house from this tree, where you were hiding by this tree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could see the house, but I was hiding from those flashlights so I didn't look at the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were able to see the light from the flashlights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the flashlights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what period of time did the gunshots last at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had moved forward some 20 metres along the creek, so that the shooting was still going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how long did the shooting last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it lasted quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other people attempt to get out of the house at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People were trying and they were killed straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could you hear from this tree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could hear crying, smoke, explosions, gunshots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there much smoke coming out of the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left this hiding place by the tree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went 20 metres, some 20 metres, further along the creek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you remain at this location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed there until the early hours of the morning, around 5.00 a.m. Of course, roughly, because I didn't have a watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this vantage point, were you able to see the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to hear any sounds coming from the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could still hear crying, shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this location, can you estimate for us how long the shooting continued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It continued for about perhaps two hours, again I'm giving an approximation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the crying that you've just mentioned, how long did that last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually leave that place and go to a village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what village did you go to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Gostilja. First we wanted to go to Babin Potok but because there were houses there, we went on to Gostilja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you remain there before leaving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Gostilja, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour at this time I'm going to ask that the witness be shown a black and white copy of Prosecution Exhibit 17.3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 84, there is a blue pen to your right in this device to your right. I'd ask you to take that blue pen -- actually I'd ask you just to make the markings on the desk in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to write VG84 at the bottom of Exhibit 17.3.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd now ask to you write the number 1 on the Memic house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask to you write the number 2 on the house which caught fire.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd now ask you to draw a circle and inside it put the initials MV to show where Mitar Vasiljevic was at the time he said that he was a representative of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've testified about hiding behind a big tree. I would ask you to approximate the location of that tree and put a circle with the number 84 to indicate where you were when you were hiding behind that tree.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, I would ask you to put a X to indicate where it was you saw people with flashlights.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay I'm going to ask that that now be placed on the ELMO and that the witness be given a pointer. Could we slide up the picture a little bit? Would I ask you, with the pointer, to indicate where you marked the house with the number 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the house that you marked number 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask to you point and hold the pointer on the circle with MV to indicate where it was you saw Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you now to point to the circle containing the number 84, to indicate where you were hiding behind the tree.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally I'd ask you to point or indicate the X where you testified you saw somebody or people with flashlights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd ask that this now be tendered into evidence as Prosecution Exhibit 17.3.VG84?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be Exhibit P17.3.VG84.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd now ask that Exhibit 17.7 be placed before the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 84, I'd ask you once again to put VG84 at the bottom of Exhibit 17.7.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'd ask to you circle the window that you pushed your mother out of and you jumped out of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I now ask that that be placed on the ELMO. I would just ask to you indicate with the pointer the window you've just circled.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness 84. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I tender that into evidence as Prosecution Exhibit 17.7.VG84. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be Exhibit P17.7.VG84. Yes, Mr. Domazet. Cross-examined by Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Sir, I have -- I'm going to ask you about a few details as to what you saw regarding the encounter between (redacted) and Mitar Vasiljevic. On that occasion, did you notice that Mitar Vasiljevic was holding a bottle in his hand? Did you see a bottle at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him holding a megaphone? I assume you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to tell me once again, to the best of your recollection, what he was wearing? Because you gave two alternative descriptions. Could you repeat what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. He had a suit on. And a hat on his head. The suit was black in colour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what he had on his feet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you looking at the time he was writing the certificate you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in the street outside the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, he was writing this certificate in the street while he was standing with Mujo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he handed it to Mujo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it raining at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was cloudy, overcast. Those days and those evenings, it did rain. At that moment, it wasn't raining.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that on your way there, you got wet because it was raining when you were coming from the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did (redacted) do with that certificate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He kept it on him. Whether he showed it to someone, to any of the people, to the other people, I don't know. I just know that he took it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't see him show it to anyone but you know that he took the certificate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see where he put the certificate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one further point: Do you remember whether Mitar Vasiljevic had any kind of ribbon on one of his sleeves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were describing the three soldiers who were in the house, and you identified two of them as being Milan and Sredoje on the basis of what others told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third soldier, did he have a mustache?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can remember, when you jumped out of this house, you mentioned that after that, you saw these flashlights and you were afraid of being discovered, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without those flashlights, could one see? Was there sufficient light? Could you have been seen without the flashlights? Or were you afraid that the flashlights would light you up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean after the fire? This is something you can't describe. There were bombs falling. Shots. The fire was spreading. There was smoke. You could -- you couldn't see that there was a house there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say that, that you couldn't see, does that mean that you couldn't see from the smoke or was it because it was dark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because of the smoke, the bomb explosions and everything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you haven't answered my question; that is, you were afraid of these flashlights lighting you up but was it possible to see without the flashlights or was it so dark that it was not possible to see without flashlights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you could see or not. Any way, they did shine the flashlights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see who was holding the flashlights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't recognise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to recognise the individual holding the flashlight, and the flashlight moved around. It flashed around the tree I was hiding behind. And I could see this light flashing in my eyes so that ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago on the photograph, you drew a circle around the window you jumped out of and according to the photograph, it is the second window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, the second one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was on the window before you jumped out, before anybody jumped out, in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was glass, reinforced glass, so when I came up to the window, I saw that VG18 was struggling to break the window. And actually, the window had already been broken but there was this netting so I just pushed that person out into the creek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the first window? Was that the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. How should I know that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking if you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you happen to see anyone jumping out of that other window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the point at which you yourself jumped out and fled towards the creek, were there any soldiers there shooting at you? There weren't. I understand you to say that there weren't any soldiers shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right and the flashlights had still not gone down by the back of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that some people were shot at and hit and killed underneath the window, below the window, did you see that personally yourself? Were you able to see that personally or did you assume that or hear it from somebody perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we went to hide behind the tree across the creek, and the flashlights were there and we passed underneath -- below them where the two windows were and we heard shooting at the windows and the screams of people at the windows. The people who had survived the explosions from the bombs and managed to jump out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Did you see this yourself directly or do you assume that that's how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I saw that from behind the tree, at one point. At one point I managed to see this. It was a split second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see in that split second?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the flashlight lighting up the windows, flashing on the windows, and that there was shooting at the windows as well. They are moments that I can't even describe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course I understand. I do understand. But I'm interested in one more thing, if you can remember. On the photograph a moment ago, you drew in the spot where you saw the flashlight throwing light on this area. Now, that individual or individuals, if there are more of them, how far away were they from that other room -- window where you saw the people jumping out of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you take the corner of the house, the edge of the house, could you determine the point where the flashlight was? You drew it for us a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, maybe I could give you an approximation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you don't have to, if you're not sure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG84 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure. I can't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for this witness, thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for coming along to give evidence. You've finished your task here and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Whilst your next witness is coming, Mr. Groome, have you filed that clearer and better response to the argument by Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, I didn't get a chance to complete it last night. I will complete it this evening and have it filed the first thing in the morning. I can fax Mr. Domazet a copy as soon as I finish it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you would, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the next witness is called, one of the items that I was going to discuss with this witness and perhaps we can come up with an alternative given the time constraint, is part of the investigation of this case there was a videotape made of the surrounding area between the two houses, the Memic house, some of the other houses and the house that caught fire in the creek. Perhaps if Mr. Domazet will agree to its admissibility the Court can look at it at its own disposal rather than taking up time now. It will take about ten to 15 minutes to show it here in court and we are prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That would be a very good idea. What do you say, Mr. Domazet? Have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have this tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will fill in our time whilst you're busy elsewhere, seeing it ourselves, if you're happy with that. Right. Well, then you can tender that. What exhibit number is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 18 it was tendered in part on the 13th of September. At this point we would tender the entire contents of videotape 18 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I hadn't realised it was admitted only in part, but that's all right. We will admit the rest of it. Where is your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Yves Roy. He should be outside the courtroom. Your Honour I'm passing what I guess is best described as a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. pseudonym sheet. The investigator will you testifying under his own name but will be referring to a number of people who have pseudonyms so for handy reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What number is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We are up to 92, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, the pseudonym sheet will be P92 and it's under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honour, my co-counsel, Mr. Tanaskovic, can he be with me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes most certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But he's in different room if somebody from security -- he's waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will get a message to him somehow. Just wait a minute. We have to get the witness sworn in. Sir, would you please take the statutory declaration in the document which the court usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir. Examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Investigator Roy, the Prosecution number 92 has given to you and it contains the names and numbers of protected witnesses. I would ask you during the course of your testimony to please refer to those witnesses by their number.

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Investigator Roy, would you please begin by describing for the Court your background?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: I joined the ICTY, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, as the investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor in June 1998. Prior to that, I was a police officer with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in Canada for 25 years. The bulk of my work with the RCMP was investigating international drug traffickers. In 1993 I was assigned with the United Nations Civilian Police, better known as UNCIVPOL in the town of Dunvar [phoen] Croatia, for seven months. I was responsible for a group of investigators, the investigation that our task was to investigate from petty theft to war crimes, location of mass graves, murders and basic human rights, investigation of basic human rights.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your work with the RCMP, would it be fair to say that you were involved in investigations in numerous countries outside of Canada?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. All the continents in the world from South America to Asia, to Europe, to Africa, everywhere in the world, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pursuant to your duties with the Office of the Prosecutor, were you assigned to investigate some of the crimes alleged to have been committed in the town of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I started, like I said earlier, started in June 1998 with the Office of the Prosecutor. Right from the start I was assigned working on numerous cases but mostly the Visegrad cases. We had to do more investigation after the arrest of Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic on the 25th of January 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with this case, the case against Mr. Vasiljevic, did you show photo arrays to several witnesses?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe briefly the general procedure that you followed when you showed photo arrays to witnesses?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: It's a really simple matter, Your Honours. When we meet witnesses, we take a full statement of the witnesses, and at the end of their statement, I show them a photo array. Usually it's from 10 to 12 pictures, of 12, 10 or 12 different men. Without telling them who I'm looking for, ask any witness if they recognise any of the men on these photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if a witness is able to recognise somebody, what procedure do you then follow?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: The procedure is again very simple. I ask the witness to sign her name on the face of the individual that they recognise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you showed VG80 such a photo array according to that procedure?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours. I did, on the 19th of January 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you show such a photo array to VG81?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: Absolutely. On the 18th of January 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you make pauses between questions and answers, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us with respect to VG38 did you also show a photo array to that witness?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours, on the 21st of June of this year, 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you describe for us how it is that you locate witnesses or how did you locate witnesses in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: Well, like in all cases, usually we get information through witnesses. They could write to the Tribunal. They could send faxes with their names on it during this period the alleged war crimes and the Office of the Prosecutor takes all these information and we -- we investigate. So that's one of the ways that we get names of witnesses when they send some information. Another way is after receiving the information from witnesses, we check our data bases here at the Tribunal and most of the time we already have received some kind of information alleging exactly the same war crimes, so at that point, we get other names of witnesses. When we go and meet witnesses, it is very seldom that they were the only witness of the alleged crime, so at the time when we take a statement, they are telling us, "Well, I was with so and so on such a date," so we learn other names of witnesses. So -- and that's -- and we made some requests to local government, it could be government from Serbia, Croatia, or Bosnia, to inquire if they have any information on these alleged crimes and most of the time they already have some information, witness names or witness statements, that they already have in hand that they provide the Tribunal with. So in a nutshell, that's the way we find witnesses usually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you specifically about witnesses VG78 and VG101, was it you that located those witnesses?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: Well, it was through investigation with our team, team at the Tribunal. The first time we heard about these two witnesses were from VG18. VG18 was mentioning that two girls have survived a fire without mentioning names. At the time VG18 didn't want to mention any names. So what we did, we made a request through our people in Bosnia to try to find the survivor of these -- of this fire on Pionirska Street and they found one of the survivors so they provided us with the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you met and interviewed both VG78 and VG101?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours. The first time when we met VG78, VG78 provided the name of VG101 so after that we went to see VG101. VG78 was interviewed on the 23rd of January of this year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: VG78. And VG101 on the 21st of March this year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VG78, did she have the same name at the time you located her as the name that she had at the time of the fire in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: No, at the time VG78 wasn't married, Your Honour, in 1992. After that she got married.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask you the same question regarding VG101?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: VG101 in 1992 wasn't married, Your Honours, and she got married after June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I've given a person's pseudonym --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could you please ask the gentlemen to slow down a bit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are all very anxious to finish but not if we kill the interpreting staff on the way. And I think that you will find if you pause, the witness will pause, and we will get along a lot more quickly in the end. Just remember what I say to all of the B/C/S speaking witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a person at the bottom of that pseudonym sheet who we've arbitrarily assigned the number VG999, one of the victims in the fire. Could you describe for us what is the relationship between VG999 and VG101 and VG78?

utterances.speaker: Yves Roy
utterances.text: VG999 is the mother of VG78 and VG101.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the original interview of VG13, did she describe seeing VG999 and her children as being victims of the Pionirska Street fire?
